title: Taiwan's F-16Vs Land as Riyadh Prepares a Red Sea Offensive and Italy Blinks on Defense Cash
subhead: Taiwan received the first two of 66 delayed F-16V Block 70s, a signal to Taipei that US arms support holds after the Xi-Trump summit. Meanwhile Saudi Arabia is preparing a Yemen offensive to retake Bab el-Mandeb, and Italy's coalition moved to cut up to 8 billion euros from its defense plan.

sections.heading: Taiwan's first F-16Vs arrive after a seven-year wait
sections.body:
The first two of the 66 F-16V Block 70 fighters Taiwan ordered from the US in 2019 touched down at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung on Friday, according to Defense News. The jets flew in via Hawaii and Guam and landed at noon local time. The $8 billion sale, approved in 2019, will eventually take Taiwan's F-16 fleet past 200 airframes; software problems had delayed delivery for years.

President Lai Ching-te thanked the US on Facebook, calling it an important step for Taiwan's air defense. Defense Minister Wellington Koo said more jets would arrive soon but gave no timeline. The delivery lands almost exactly a week after Trump met Xi Jinping in Washington, and after Trump said in May that he was holding a new $14 billion Taiwan package in abeyance — though he did approve one worth $11 billion in December 2025.

The SCMP framed the arrival as Taipei's evidence that US support still holds after the summit. Reuters, citing people familiar with US thinking, reports that US officials now consider a Chinese invasion before 2028 — Taiwan's next presidential election year — increasingly unlikely. Koo nonetheless said 'China's intention to annex Taiwan by force has never changed.'
sections.whyItMatters: A $8B sale stuck for seven years finally shipping is as much a political message as a capability gain. It tests whether Washington can keep arming Taipei while managing Beijing — and whether Taiwan's long F-16 backorder finally clears.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia prepares a Yemen offensive to reopen Bab el-Mandeb
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia is planning an offensive against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, with options including a coastal push to secure the Red Sea route or synchronized attacks on multiple fronts, regional and Western officials told Reuters. The operation, expected within weeks, would be led by Yemeni forces on the ground overseen by Riyadh and backed by Saudi airstrikes; the US is already providing intelligence, and some European and regional states give mainly defensive aid.

The trigger is last month's Houthi advance down the coast and their seizure of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the Red Sea's southern exit. That passage has gained importance as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, effectively closed by the Iran conflict. Riyadh, the officials said, has concluded it cannot enter new peace talks while the Houthis hold the strait.

Scale could reach 100,000 Yemeni troops, depending on the option chosen. Timing estimates range from within a week to after the US midterm elections in early November. Saudi, Yemeni, Houthi and US military spokespeople did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a maritime-chokepoint play, not a civil-war redux. With Hormuz shut, Bab el-Mandeb is the last functioning Red Sea artery — and whoever controls it holds leverage over Gulf energy exports and global shipping premiums.

sections.heading: Italy's coalition moves to claw back up to 8 billion euros from defense
sections.body:
Italian military planners risk losing up to 8 billion euros ($9 billion) in funding as government and opposition parties push to cut both defense spending and support for Ukraine, Defense News reports. At a Thursday Cabinet meeting, deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini succeeded in pushing down the defense windfall from the EU's National Escape Clause — which lets states exempt rearmament spending from deficit rules — from roughly 21-22 billion euros to about 14 billion.

Salvini's League opposes defense hikes and wants a deal with Moscow; to Meloni's right, Roberto Vannacci wants sanctions on Russia lifted. On the left, the Five Star party blames 'war-mongering Europe' for the conflict — a poll of its members found over 90% opposed European rearmament and believed arms to Ukraine prolonged the war. A government source told Defense News the reduction was 'yet to be made definite but... agreed.'

Despite the squeeze, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has committed to NATO's 5% of GDP target and claims Italy already reached 2.8% this year, counting domestic security spending.
sections.whyItMatters: Italy is the clearest test of whether NATO's new spending targets survive domestic politics. Meloni has committed to the numbers but cannot hold her own coalition to them — a warning for other European governments whose rearmament plans rest on fragile majorities.

sections.heading: France bets on sovereign AI for its first loyal wingman flight in 2028
sections.body:
France's Air Force, the Directorate General for Armament (DGA) and its defense AI agency Amiad plan to fly crewed fighters alongside combat drones in 2028 under a project called Hypairion, Defense News reports. The aim is open, modular architecture and sovereign AI that keeps the state — not industry — in control of critical systems.

'What Hypairion is really about is equipping the Air Force and our platforms with architectures that are open, modular and owned by the government,' said Col. Cedric, head of the Air Force capability-development office. The project deliberately diverges from company-driven efforts by Airbus, BAE Systems, General Atomics and Anduril. Two Mirage 2000s at Mont-de-Marsan are being modified into AI test beds, with testing to start by year-end.

The 2028 unmanned platform is a test article, not necessarily the future Rafale wingman under the F5 standard, targeted by the DGA around 2033. Amiad already applies AI in the Army's Pendragon robotics project.
sections.whyItMatters: Most loyal-wingman programs are prime-contractor led. France is building state-owned control of the architecture instead, a bid to avoid vendor lock-in as European collaborative combat aircraft efforts proliferate.

sections.heading: China's PLA overhauls its academies around AI, drones and discipline
sections.body:
China's People's Liberation Army is restructuring its military academy colleges to build a technical workforce and tighten its anti-corruption drive, with new colleges dedicated to AI and drones, according to the South China Morning Post. The reform is presented as a workforce-and-discipline push rather than a battlefield announcement.

It comes alongside the SCMP's reporting that the US says its F-47 will be the first sixth-generation fighter, while China's J-36 and J-50 prototypes are already flying — a pointed counter to US claims of a generational lead. The same outlet noted a SCMP analysis that US HIMARS munitions shortfalls raise the stakes for any Taiwan Strait conflict.
sections.whyItMatters: China is investing in the institutional layer that turns commercial AI and drone know-how into military output. Academy reform is slow to show up in inventories but it is how the PLA converts industrial strength into doctrine — and it frames the F-47 versus J-36/J-50 contest as an institutional race, not just a platform one.

sections.heading: Russia drills FPV drone swarms as CSTO exercises close
sections.body:
Russia's Center-2026 strategic command exercise practiced FPV drone crews operating in a 'swarm' formation against motorcycle-borne assault groups at the Chebarkul training ground, the Defense Ministry said via TASS. The drills at Chebarkul involved more than 6,000 military personnel — 4,600 Russian and 1,479 foreign, including 634 from CSTO rapid-reaction forces — plus more than 600 pieces of equipment, 55 aircraft and helicopters, over 500 drones of various types, and more than 50 robotic systems.

TASS separately reported that the active phase of the CSTO's Interaction-2026, Poisk-2026 and Echelon-2026 exercises finished on Russian territory, with troops drilling recon, fire superiority, urban clearing and border-control restoration using drones and robotics 'based on the experience of the special military operation.' A Caspian Flotilla live-fire drill against a maritime target — using the Tatarstan missile ship and the Bal coastal missile system — was also part of Center-2026.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia is formalizing drone and robotics tactics learned in Ukraine into allied CSTO doctrine. FPV swarms and counter-drone mobile fire groups are now exercise-benchmarked, not improvised — a sign the lessons are hardening into standard doctrine for Moscow and its partners.

sections.heading: French Army reorganizes artillery and armor to survive drone-heavy battlefields
sections.body:
Two Defense News reports show the French Army reworking its ground formations around the drone threat: one artillery regiment has reorganized its guns to survive drone attacks, and France is experimenting with smaller tank units to evade drones. The changes treat massed, static formations as liabilities in a battlefield saturated with cheap aerial observation and strike drones.

The moves track with a broader European pattern of adapting armor and artillery to low-cost drone surveillance and loitering munitions, moving toward dispersal and concealment rather than concentrated firepower.
sections.whyItMatters: Western armies are beginning to change force structure, not just add counter-drone gadgets. Dispersing tanks and re-siting guns is an organizational admission that cheap drones have permanently altered how armor and artillery can mass.

bottomLine: Taiwan received the first two of 66 F-16V Block 70s after a seven-year delay, a delivery Taipei read as proof US arms support survives the Xi-Trump summit — even as Washington weighs a $14B package in abeyance. In the Gulf, Saudi Arabia is preparing a Yemen offensive to retake Bab el-Mandeb, now the last working Red Sea artery with Hormuz shut. And in Europe, Italy's coalition moved to strip up to 8 billion euros from its defense plan, the clearest sign yet that NATO's new spending targets are colliding with domestic politics. On the industrial side, France is building state-owned AI architecture for a 2028 loyal wingman, China is restructuring PLA academies around AI and drones, and Russia is benchmarking FPV drone swarms into CSTO doctrine. The through-line is adaptation: forces and institutions are reorganizing around drones and delivery bottlenecks faster than budgets can be locked in.
sources: Defense News, Reuters, South China Morning Post, TASS, Breaking Defense
